newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Mkt not fully priced for 2nd hike.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Mkt not fully priced for 2nd hike.

text.p: Despite growing expectations the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates further, the U.S. Treasury market yield curve showed little movement on Wednesday, suggesting the market might take time to fully factor in another tightening.
The two-year to 30-year spread was unchanged at 62 basis points on Wednesday. After the Federal Reserve's rate hike on Tuesday, it had narrowed to 62 from 66 on Monday.
The Fed raised its target rate on Tuesday to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent. Market participants are leaning toward the Fed tightening again at either its May or July meetings.

For the spread to flatten further, "the market needs to discount further rate hikes down the road and it hasn't done that yet," said Tom Macirowski, senior Treasury market strategist at Goldman Sachs & Co.
Analysts expect the two-year to 30-year spread to flatten another seven to 10 basis points in the next few months.
Macirowski noted the two-year note, at 6.37 percent, is only 87 basis points above the new federal funds target.

"That's not exactly bearish," Macirowski said. "I would think 100 basis points is definitely doable as the market gets Macirowski said that the five-year to 30-year spread should flatten more than two-year to 30-year, with the two-year to five-year spread steepening somewhat. The five-year to 30-year spread stood at 33 basis points late Wednesday, from 32 basis points Tuesday.

With the exception of bills, Treasury yields rose on Wednesday after Commerce reported a robust 1.5 percent jump in February durable goods orders following a very strong 4.1 percent rise in January. Selling in futures later added to the losses.
Players said the data confirmed that Fed policy makers were on target in hiking rates at the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).
"I am not surprised the bond market has not taken this real well," said Ethan Harris, senior economist at Lehman Brothers.
"The problem for the market is that nothing in (its policy) statement said whether it was a one-time move. It (suggested) that if growth remains strong they will move again," Harris said.
Still, analysts said May might be too soon for the Fed to move again, so the market for now is setting its sights on early July for another rate hike.
"There will be a lot of focus on growth indicators," Harris said. So, "I think the market will stay in a bad mood for a while."
